concepts: Inequalities in the Argand plane with $\mathrm{Re}$ and $\mathrm{Im}$ of a complex expression
questions.question:
For $a\in\mathbb{C}$, let $A=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:\mathrm{Re}(a+\bar z)>\mathrm{Im}(\bar a+z)\}$ and $B=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:\mathrm{Re}(a+\bar z)<\mathrm{Im}(\bar a+z)\}$. Then among the two statements:
(S1): If $\mathrm{Re}(a),\mathrm{Im}(a)>0$, then the set $A$ contains all the real numbers.
(S2): If $\mathrm{Re}(a),\mathrm{Im}(a)<0$, then the set $B$ contains all the real numbers.
questions.key_idea: Writing $a=x_1+iy_1$, $z=x+iy$ turns each set into a half-plane, and one real $z$ outside it disproves the statement.
solution: Then $x_1+x=-10$ and $-y_1+y=-10$, so the strict inequality $-10>-10$ is not valid: $z=-12\notin A$.
Hence $A$ does not contain all real numbers: S1 is false.
Then $x_1+x=10$ and $-y_1+y=10$, so $10<10$ is not valid: $z=12\notin B$.
Hence S2 is false too. Both statements are false: option (B).

alternate_solutions.idea: Each set is an open half-plane bounded by a line of slope $1$; the real axis crosses that line, so it cannot lie wholly inside either set.
solution: The boundary of both is the line $x-y=-(x_1+y_1)$, which has slope $1$.
$A$ and $B$ are the two open half-planes on either side of this line.
The real axis $y=0$ has slope $0$, so it is not parallel to the boundary and meets it at $x=-(x_1+y_1)$.
A line that crosses the boundary has points on both sides, so the real axis lies in neither half-plane completely.
For real $z=x$: $A\cap\mathbb{R}=\{x>-(x_1+y_1)\}$ and $B\cap\mathbb{R}=\{x<-(x_1+y_1)\}$, each only a half-line.
This holds for every $a$, so both statements are false: option (B).

useful_results: $\mathrm{Re}(a+\bar z)=x_1+x$ and $\mathrm{Im}(\bar a+z)=y-y_1$: a linear inequality in $x,y$ always describes a half-plane.
A line (here the real axis) lies wholly inside an open half-plane only if it is parallel to the boundary and on the correct side; a transversal line never does.
To disprove a 'contains all reals' claim, test one real $z$ on the boundary (equality makes a strict inequality fail), e.g. $z=-(x_1+y_1)$ for $A$.

concepts: Collinear points and the circle in the Argand plane (product of distances from the centre)
questions.question: Let $C$ be the circle in the complex plane with centre $z_0=\frac12(1+3i)$ and radius $r=1$. Let $z_1=1+i$ and the complex number $z_2$ be outside the circle $C$ such that $|z_1-z_0||z_2-z_0|=1$. If $z_0,z_1$ and $z_2$ are collinear, then the smaller value of $|z_2|^2$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $|z_1-z_0|=\frac1{\sqrt2}$ forces $|z_2-z_0|=\sqrt2$, so $z_2$ lies on the line $z_0z_1$ at distance $\sqrt2$ from $z_0$, on either side.
solution: From $|z_1-z_0||z_2-z_0|=1$: $|z_2-z_0|=\sqrt2$, and the centre is $z_0\left(\frac12,\frac32\right)$ with $z_1(1,1)$.
The line through $z_0$ and $z_1$ has slope $\frac{1-3/2}{1-1/2}=-1$, so $\tan\theta=-1$ and $\theta=135^\circ$.

$z_2$ is at distance $\sqrt2$ from $z_0$ along this line: $z_2=\left(\frac12+\sqrt2\cos135^\circ,\ \frac32+\sqrt2\sin135^\circ\right)$ or $\left(\frac12-\sqrt2\cos135^\circ,\ \frac32-\sqrt2\sin135^\circ\right)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Collinearity means $z_2-z_0=t(z_1-z_0)$ with real $t$; the product condition fixes $|t|=2$, so $z_2=2z_1-z_0$ or $3z_0-2z_1$ with no angles.
solution: $|z_2|^2$ is $\frac94+\frac14=\frac52$ for the first and $\frac14+\frac{25}{4}=\frac{13}2$ for the second.

useful_results: $|z_1-z_0||z_2-z_0|=r^2$ with $z_0,z_1,z_2$ collinear and $z_1,z_2$ on the same side of $z_0$ means $z_2$ is the inverse of $z_1$ in the circle of radius $r$ about $z_0$: $z_2-z_0=\frac{r^2}{\overline{z_1-z_0}}$.
The question also allows $z_2$ on the opposite side of $z_0$, so two answers appear; read 'smaller/larger' as a hint that both are meant.
Collinear points: $z_2-z_0=t(z_1-z_0)$ with $t\in\mathbb{R}$; this avoids slopes and angles.

concepts: Polar form and powers of the roots of a quadratic with complex roots
questions.question: Let $\alpha,\beta$ be the roots of the equation $x^2-\sqrt2x+2=0$. Then $\alpha^{14}+\beta^{14}$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Write the roots as $\sqrt2e^{\pm i\pi/3}$; then $\alpha^{14}+\beta^{14}=2\cdot2^7\cos\frac{14\pi}{3}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: From $\alpha^2=\sqrt2\alpha-2$ get $\alpha^3=-2\sqrt2$ for both roots, so $\alpha^{14}=(\alpha^3)^4\alpha^2$ and the sum reduces to $64(\alpha^2+\beta^2)$.

useful_results: A quadratic $x^2-px+q=0$ with $p^2<4q$ has roots $\sqrt q\,e^{\pm i\theta}$ with $\cos\theta=\frac{p}{2\sqrt q}$; then $\alpha^n+\beta^n=2q^{n/2}\cos n\theta$.
If $\alpha^3$ turns out to be real (here $-2\sqrt2$), every high power reduces to $\alpha^{3k+r}$; check by squaring or by $\arg\alpha=\frac{\pi}{3}$.
Quick check for this instance: $\theta=\frac\pi3$, $n=14$, $\cos\frac{14\pi}{3}=\cos\frac{2\pi}{3}=-\frac12$.

concepts: Solving an equation in $z$, $\bar z$ and $\mathrm{Re}(z)$ by separating real and imaginary parts
questions.question: Let $S=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:\bar z=i(z^2+\mathrm{Re}(\bar z))\}$. Then $\sum_{z\in S}|z|^2$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Put $z=x+iy$ and split into real and imaginary parts: the real part gives $x(2y+1)=0$, a product of two lines.
solution: Let $z=x+iy$, so $\mathrm{Re}(\bar z)=x$ and $\bar z=i(z^2+x)$ becomes $x-iy=i(x^2-y^2+2ixy+x)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Equation (ii) factors as $(x+y)(x-y+1)=0$, so the solutions are the intersections of two pairs of lines.
solution: With $z=x+iy$ the two real equations are $x(2y+1)=0$ and $x^2+x-y^2+y=0$.
Factor the second: $x^2-y^2+(x+y)=(x+y)(x-y+1)=0$, i.e. the lines $y=-x$ and $y=x+1$.
The first gives the lines $x=0$ and $y=-\frac12$.

useful_results: For equations in $z,\bar z$, write $z=x+iy$ and treat the real and imaginary parts as two curves; factorising one often turns the problem into intersecting lines.
A homogeneous-looking quadratic like $x^2-y^2+(x+y)$ factors as $(x+y)(x-y+1)$ because $x^2-y^2=(x+y)(x-y)$.
Always substitute the candidate points back: here $z=i$ gives $\bar z=-i=i(i^2+0)$, confirming it.

concepts: Intersection of a circle and a line in the Argand plane
questions.question: Let $A=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z-2-i|=3\}$, $B=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:\mathrm{Re}(z-iz)=2\}$ and $S=A\cap B$. Then $\sum_{z\in S}|z|^2$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: $\mathrm{Re}(z-iz)=x+y$, so $B$ is the line $x+y=2$ cutting the circle $A$ in two points; sum $|z|^2$ over them.
solution: $x^2=\frac{26\pm6\sqrt{17}}{4}$ and $y^2=\frac{18\mp2\sqrt{17}}{4}$; the surds cancel when the two points are added.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the circle's equation to write $|z|^2=4x+2y+4$, then only $\sum x$ and $\sum y$ (Vieta) are needed - no surds.
solution: The circle $(x-2)^2+(y-1)^2=9$ gives $x^2+y^2=4x+2y+4$ for every point of $A$.
So on $S$: $|z|^2=4x+2y+4$, and $\sum_{z\in S}|z|^2=4\sum x+2\sum y+8$ (two points).
The line $x+y=2$ meets the circle where $x^2-3x-2=0$, so $x_1+x_2=3$.

useful_results: For a circle $|z-c|=r$, $|z|^2=2\mathrm{Re}(\bar c z)+r^2-|c|^2$: on the circle, $|z|^2$ is linear in $x,y$, so sums over intersection points follow from Vieta.
Sum of $|z|^2$ over the two intersection points of a line and circle is symmetric in the roots - no need to find the points.
$\mathrm{Re}(z-iz)=\mathrm{Re}\{(1-i)z\}=x+y$: multiplying by $1-i$ and taking the real part gives a line of slope $-1$.

concepts: Cube roots of unity and sums of powers
questions.question: If $\alpha$ is a root of the equation $x^2+x+1=0$ and $\sum_{k=1}^{n}\left(\alpha^k+\frac1{\alpha^k}\right)^2=20$, then $n$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: $\alpha=\omega$ or $\omega^2$, so each term is $(-1)^2=1$ unless $3\mid k$, when it is $2^2=4$ (period 3).
solution: $\alpha=\omega$ or $\omega^2$ (the answer is the same for both).
Terms $k=1,\dots,11$: $k=3,6,9$ give $4$ each ($12$) and the other eight give $1$ each ($8$), total $20$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Expand each square: $\sum\left(\alpha^{2k}+\alpha^{-2k}+2\right)=2n+2\mathrm{Re}\sum\alpha^{2k}$ and evaluate the geometric sum by the residue of $n$ mod $3$.
solution: $\left(\alpha^k+\alpha^{-k}\right)^2=\alpha^{2k}+\alpha^{-2k}+2$, so the sum is $2n+\sum_{k=1}^{n}\left(\omega^{2k}+\omega^{-2k}\right)$ and the last part is real.
Any three consecutive $k$ give $\omega^{2k}$ summing to $0$ (powers of a cube root of unity), so only the leftover $n\bmod3$ terms matter.
$n\equiv0$: leftover $0$, sum $=2n=20$ gives $n=10$, not a multiple of $3$ - rejected.
$n\equiv1$: leftover term $\omega^{2n}+\omega^{-2n}=-1$, so $2n-1=20$ has no integer solution.
$n\equiv2$: the two leftover terms contribute $-1-1=-2$ (each $\omega^{2k}+\omega^{-2k}=-1$ for $3\nmid k$), so $2n-2=20$ and $n=11$, and $11\equiv2$ checks.

useful_results: For $\omega$ a primitive cube root of unity, $\omega^k+\omega^{-k}=2$ if $3\mid k$ and $-1$ otherwise; any sum of powers is periodic with period $3$.
$1+\omega+\omega^2=0$ and $\omega^3=1$: a full block of three consecutive powers sums to $0$.
When the summand is periodic, compute one period's sum, then use the quotient and remainder of $n$ by the period.

concepts: Binomial expansion (odd-indexed binomial coefficients)
Cube roots of unity and powers of $1\pm\sqrt3 i$
questions.question: If $\alpha=1+\sum_{r=1}^{6}(-3)^{r-1}\,{}^{12}C_{2r-1}$, then the distance of the point $\left(12,\sqrt3\right)$ from the line $\alpha x-\sqrt3y+1=0$ is ______.
questions.key_idea: With $x=\sqrt3 i$, $(-3)^{r-1}=\frac{x^{2r-1}}{x}$, so the sum is the odd part of $(1+x)^{12}$ divided by $x$.
solution: Let $x=\sqrt3 i$. Then $(-3)^{r-1}=\frac{\left(\sqrt3 i\right)^{2r-1}}{\sqrt3 i}$, so $\alpha=1+\frac{1}{\sqrt3 i}\left({}^{12}C_1x+{}^{12}C_3x^3+\dots+{}^{12}C_{11}x^{11}\right)$.
The bracket is the odd part of the expansion: $\frac{(1+x)^{12}-(1-x)^{12}}{2}$.
$1+\sqrt3 i=-2\omega^2$ and $1-\sqrt3 i=-2\omega$, so the numerator is $\left(-2\omega^2\right)^{12}-\left(-2\omega\right)^{12}=2^{12}-2^{12}=0$ (as $\omega^{24}=\omega^{12}=1$).

alternate_solutions.idea: Take the imaginary part of $\left(1+i\sqrt3\right)^{12}$ in polar form: $2e^{i\pi/3}$ raised to $12$ is real, so the odd-index sum is $0$.
solution: $\left(1+i\sqrt3\right)^{12}=\sum_k{}^{12}C_k\left(i\sqrt3\right)^k$, and the imaginary part comes from odd $k=2r-1$.
In polar form $1+i\sqrt3=2e^{i\pi/3}$, so $\left(1+i\sqrt3\right)^{12}=2^{12}e^{i4\pi}=4096$, a real number.
Hence its imaginary part is $0$, so $\sum(-3)^{r-1}\,{}^{12}C_{2r-1}=0$ and $\alpha=1$.

useful_results: Odd-index binomial sums: $\sum_k{}^nC_{2k+1}x^{2k+1}=\frac{(1+x)^n-(1-x)^n}{2}$; even-index: $\frac{(1+x)^n+(1-x)^n}{2}$.

Alternating-sign sums such as $\sum(-3)^{r}{}^nC_{2r}$ or $\sum(-1)^r 3^r\,{}^nC_{2r+1}$ are real/imaginary parts of $\left(1+i\sqrt3\right)^n$ or $\left(1+i\right)^n$: recognise the powers $(\sqrt3 i)^{2r}=(-3)^r$.
$1+i\sqrt3=2e^{i\pi/3}=-2\omega^2$ and $1-i\sqrt3=2e^{-i\pi/3}=-2\omega$; $\left(1\pm i\sqrt3\right)^n$ is real when $6\mid n$ (here $n=12$).

concepts: Determinant with cube roots of unity as entries
Locus $|z-a|=|z+b|$ (perpendicular bisector) in the Argand plane
questions.question: Let integers $a,b\in[-3,3]$ be such that $a+b\neq0$. Then the number of all possible ordered pairs $(a,b)$, for which $\left|\frac{z-a}{z+b}\right|=1$ and $\left|\begin{matrix} z+1&\omega&\omega^2\\ \omega&z+\omega^2&1\\ \omega^2&1&z+\omega\end{matrix}\right|=1$, $z\in\mathbb{C}$, where $\omega$ and $\omega^2$ are the roots of $x^2+x+1=0$, is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: The determinant equals $z^3$, so $z$ is a cube root of unity; then $|z-a|=|z+b|$ must hold for $z=1$ or $z=\omega,\omega^2$, each giving a line $b=a+\text{const}$.
solution: Operate $R_1\to R_1+R_2+R_3$ (using $1+\omega+\omega^2=0$): the first row becomes $z,\ z,\ z$.
The two families ($b=a-2$ and $b=a+1$) do not overlap, so the number of ordered pairs is $4+6=10$.
questions.correction_note: PDF stops at $z^3=1$ and writes 'Now $|1-a|=|1+b|$ $\Rightarrow$ 10 pairs': it treats only $z=1$ (which alone gives 4 pairs) and gives no count. The counting for $z=1$ and for $z=\omega,\omega^2$ (6 pairs) was missing and has been added; the answer 10 is correct (verified by brute force).

alternate_solutions.idea: The matrix is $zI+vv^T$ with $v=(1,\omega,\omega^2)^T$ (rank one), so its determinant is $z^3+z^2\,v^Tv=z^3$; then $|z-a|=|z+b|$ says $z$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of the real points $a$ and $-b$.
solution: The matrix equals $zI+N$ where $N_{ij}=\omega^{i+j}$ (indices $0,1,2$), i.e. $N=vv^T$ with $v=(1,\omega,\omega^2)^T$: rank one.
For a rank-one update, $\det(zI+vv^T)=z^3+z^2\,(v^Tv)$, and $v^Tv=1+\omega^2+\omega^4=1+\omega^2+\omega=0$, so the determinant is $z^3$.
$z^3=1$ gives the three points $1,\ \omega,\ \omega^2$ (vertices of an equilateral triangle on the unit circle).
$|z-a|=|z+b|$ says $z$ is equidistant from the real points $a$ and $-b$: it lies on their perpendicular bisector, the vertical line $x=\frac{a-b}{2}$ (since $a\neq-b$).
$z=1$ lies on this line when $\frac{a-b}{2}=1$, i.e. $b=a-2$: $(-1,-3),(0,-2),(2,0),(3,1)$ and the rejected $(1,-1)$: $4$ pairs.
$z=\omega,\omega^2$ have real part $-\frac12$, so $\frac{a-b}{2}=-\frac12$, i.e. $b=a+1$: $a=-3,\dots,2$ gives $6$ pairs, none with $a+b=0$.

useful_results: Circulant-type shortcut: adding all rows into one row (or using $1+\omega+\omega^2=0$) pulls out a factor $z$; for a matrix $zI+N$ with $N$ of rank one, $\det=z^3+z^2\,\mathrm{tr}N$.
$|z-p|=|z-q|$ for real $p\neq q$ is the vertical line $\mathrm{Re}\,z=\frac{p+q}{2}$; here $p=a$, $q=-b$, so $\mathrm{Re}\,z=\frac{a-b}{2}$.
Roots of $z^3=1$ have real parts $1,-\frac12,-\frac12$, so only the two values $\frac{a-b}2=1$ or $-\frac12$ matter; count lattice pairs on each line and remove those with $a+b=0$.

concepts: Roots of a polynomial and factorisation $P(x)=4\prod(x-x_k)$
Modulus of a complex number
questions.question: Let $x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4$ be the solutions of the equation $4x^4+8x^3-17x^2-12x+9=0$ and $\left(4+x_1^2\right)\left(4+x_2^2\right)\left(4+x_3^2\right)\left(4+x_4^2\right)=\frac{125}{16}m$. Then the value of $m$ is ______.
questions.key_idea: $4+x_k^2=|2i-x_k|^2$ for real roots, so evaluate the polynomial at $x=2i$ and take its modulus.
solution: Square both sides: $141^2+88^2=16\prod|2i-x_k|^2=16\prod\left(4+x_k^2\right)$ (true as the coefficients are real, so roots are real or in conjugate pairs).

alternate_solutions.idea: Factor the quartic by the rational-root test: $(x+1)(x+3)(2x-1)(2x-3)$, then multiply $4+x^2$ over the four roots directly.

useful_results: $\prod\left(x_k^2+k^2\right)=\frac{|P(ik)|^2}{a_n^2}$ for a real polynomial $P=a_n\prod(x-x_k)$: $\prod(x_k-ik)(x_k+ik)=\frac{P(ik)P(-ik)}{a_n^2}=\frac{|P(ik)|^2}{a_n^2}$.
Products such as $\prod(a-x_k)$ are just $\frac{P(a)}{a_n}$; evaluating at a convenient (possibly complex) point avoids finding the roots.
For quartics with integer coefficients try rational roots $\pm\frac{p}{q}$ ($p\mid9$, $q\mid4$ here) first - a full factorisation is often available.

concepts: Lattice points in a region of the Argand plane (disc and perpendicular-bisector half-plane)
questions.question: The sum of the squares of the modulus of the elements in the set $\{z=a+ib:\ a,b\in\mathbb{Z},\ z\in\mathbb{C},\ |z-1|\le1,\ |z-5|\le|z-5i|\}$ is ______.
questions.key_idea: $|z-5|\le|z-5i|$ is the half-plane $b\le a$; list the lattice points of the unit disc about $1$ that lie in it.
solution: $|z-1|\le1$: the closed disc with centre $(1,0)$ and radius $1$.
$|z-5|\le|z-5i|$: $z$ is at least as near to $5$ as to $5i$, i.e. $(a-5)^2+b^2\le a^2+(b-5)^2$, which simplifies to $b\le a$ (the half-plane on or below the line $y=x$).
Each satisfies $b\le a$: $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$ lie on the line $y=x$, and the others lie below it.

alternate_solutions.idea: On the lattice points of the disc, $(a-1)^2+b^2\in\{0,1\}$ gives $a^2+b^2=2a-1$ or $2a$, so the required sum needs only the values of $a$.
solution: Expanding, $a^2+b^2=2a-1+\left[(a-1)^2+b^2\right]$: it is $2a-1$ for the centre and $2a$ for the four points at distance $1$.
The condition $|z-5|\le|z-5i|$ reduces to $b\le a$, which holds for the centre $(1,0)$ and for all four neighbours $(0,0),(2,0),(1,1),(1,-1)$.

useful_results: $|z-p|\le|z-q|$ is the closed half-plane on the side of $p$ of the perpendicular bisector of $p$ and $q$; for $p=5,q=5i$ the bisector is $y=x$.
Lattice points of a disc of radius $1$ about an integer point: exactly $5$ (the centre and its four neighbours).
On a circle $|z-c|=r$ with real $c$, $|z|^2=2c\,\mathrm{Re}\,z+r^2-c^2$: $|z|^2$ becomes linear in $a$.

concepts: Cube roots of unity: reducing powers of $\alpha$
Binomial expansion of $(1+\alpha)^7$
questions.question: If $\alpha$ satisfies the equation $x^2+x+1=0$ and $(1+\alpha)^7=A+B\alpha+C\alpha^2$, $A,B,C\ge0$, then $5(3A-2B-C)$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: Since $1+\alpha+\alpha^2=0$, $(A,B,C)$ can shift by $(t,t,t)$ without changing the number, and $3A-2B-C$ is unchanged by that shift.
questions.correction_note: The PDF's second line reads $1+7\alpha+21\alpha^2+35\alpha^3+35\alpha^4+24\alpha^5+7\alpha^6+\alpha^9$: the coefficient ${}^7C_5=21$ (not 24) and the last term is $\alpha^7$ (not $\alpha^9$). Its next line has the correct values, so the final working and the answer are unchanged. The PDF also does not mention that $A,B,C$ are not unique (any $(A+t,B+t,C+t)$ works because $1+\alpha+\alpha^2=0$); the expression asked is the same for all of them.

alternate_solutions.idea: $1+\alpha=-\alpha^2$, so $(1+\alpha)^7=-\alpha^{14}=-\alpha^2=1+\alpha$: read off $(A,B,C)=(1,1,0)$ at once; every other valid triple differs by $(t,t,t)$, which leaves $3A-2B-C$ unchanged.
solution: Any other representation differs by $t(1+\alpha+\alpha^2)=0$, i.e. $(A,B,C)\to(A+t,B+t,C+t)$; then $3A-2B-C\to3A-2B-C+t(3-2-1)=3A-2B-C$, unchanged.

useful_results: $1+\omega=-\omega^2$ and $1+\omega^2=-\omega$: $(1+\omega)^n=(-1)^n\omega^{2n}$ - one line instead of a full binomial expansion.

Because $1+\omega+\omega^2=0$, the representation $A+B\omega+C\omega^2$ is not unique; only differences like $A-C$ and $B-C$ are determined. Check that the asked expression is invariant (here the coefficients $3,-2,-1$ sum to $0$).
Sum of binomial coefficients by residue class: $\sum_{k\equiv j\ (3)}{}^nC_k$ gives the coefficients $A,B,C$ of the expansion of $(1+\omega)^n$ before reducing.

concepts: Circle in the Argand plane and the inverse point $\frac1{\bar\alpha}$ (modulus relations)
questions.question: Let the complex numbers $\alpha$ and $\frac{1}{\bar\alpha}$ lie on the circles $|z-z_0|^2=4$ and $|z-z_0|^2=16$ respectively, where $z_0=1+i$. Then the value of $100|\alpha|^2$ is ______.
questions.key_idea: Expand both circle conditions: the cross term $\alpha\bar z_0+\bar\alpha z_0$ appears in both and can be eliminated, leaving an equation in $|\alpha|^2$ only.
solution: $|\alpha|^2-\alpha\bar z_0-\bar\alpha z_0+|z_0|^2=4$, and $|z_0|^2=2$, so $|\alpha|^2-\alpha\bar z_0-\bar\alpha z_0=2$ ......(i)

alternate_solutions.idea: Use polar form $\alpha=re^{i\theta}$, $z_0=\sqrt2e^{i\pi/4}$: both circle conditions contain the same $\cos\left(\theta-\frac\pi4\right)$, which is eliminated.

useful_results: $\frac1{\bar\alpha}$ is the inverse of $\alpha$ in the unit circle: it lies on the same ray from $0$ and $\left|\frac1{\bar\alpha}\right|=\frac1{|\alpha|}$.
For two conditions on $\alpha$ built from the same cross term $\mathrm{Re}(\alpha\bar z_0)$, eliminate that term by subtraction or substitution rather than solving for $\alpha$.
$|w-z_0|^2=|w|^2-2\mathrm{Re}(w\bar z_0)+|z_0|^2$ is the working formula; keep $|z_0|^2=2$ for $z_0=1+i$.

concepts: Reducing powers of the roots of a quadratic using the equation $x^2=x-2$
questions.question: Let $\alpha,\beta$ be the roots of the equation $x^2-x+2=0$ with $\mathrm{Im}(\alpha)>\mathrm{Im}(\beta)$. Then $\alpha^6+\alpha^4+\beta^4-5\alpha^2$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: Reduce $x^6$ and $x^4$ using $x^2+2=x$ so the expression becomes a function of $\alpha^2+\beta^2=1-4$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Reduce every power to the form $px+q$ by repeatedly using $x^2=x-2$, then apply $\alpha+\beta=1$.

useful_results: For a quadratic root $x$, every power $x^n$ reduces to $p_nx+q_n$ via $x^2=sx-p$; then sums over both roots need only $\alpha+\beta$ and $\alpha\beta$.
Sums of equal powers of both roots: $\alpha^n+\beta^n=s\,S_{n-1}-p\,S_{n-2}$ (here $S_n=S_{n-1}-2S_{n-2}$), giving $S_2=-3$, $S_4=1$.
The ordering condition $\mathrm{Im}\,\alpha>\mathrm{Im}\,\beta$ is irrelevant when the expression's $\alpha^6,\alpha^2$ part reduces to a constant (here $12$); check this before choosing a root.

concepts: Polar form and powers of the roots of a quadratic with complex roots
questions.question: Let $\alpha,\beta$ be the roots of the equation $x^2-\sqrt6x+3=0$ such that $\mathrm{Im}(\alpha)>\mathrm{Im}(\beta)$. Let $a,b$ be integers not divisible by $3$ and $n$ be a natural number such that $\frac{\alpha^{99}}{\beta}+\alpha^{98}=3^n(a+ib)$, $i=\sqrt{-1}$. Then $n+a+b$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: Factor $\alpha^{98}\left(\frac\alpha\beta+1\right)=\frac{\alpha^{98}(\alpha+\beta)}{\beta}$ and use the polar forms $\sqrt3e^{\pm i\pi/4}$.
solution: $n=49,\ a=-1,\ b=1$ (neither $a$ nor $b$ is divisible by $3$).

alternate_solutions.idea: $\frac\alpha\beta=e^{i\pi/2}=i$ and $\alpha^2=3i$, so the whole expression is $(\alpha^2)^{49}(i+1)$ with no large angles.

useful_results: If $\alpha=\sqrt{q}\,e^{i\theta}$, $\beta=\bar\alpha$ then $\frac\alpha\beta=e^{2i\theta}$ and $\alpha^2=qe^{2i\theta}$; for $\theta=\frac\pi4$ these are $i$ and $qi$, so even powers cycle through $\pm1,\pm i$.
Reduce large angles mod $2\pi$ first: $\frac{99\pi}{4}\equiv\frac{3\pi}{4}$; or reduce the exponent of $i$ mod $4$.
$\alpha+\beta=2\mathrm{Re}\,\alpha$ and $\alpha\beta=|\alpha|^2$ for conjugate roots: $\sqrt6$ and $3$ here.

concepts: Simplifying complex expressions, modulus and argument
Number of solutions of an exponential equation
questions.question: If $\alpha$ denotes the number of solutions of $|1-i|^x=2^x$ and $\beta=\left(\frac{|z|}{\arg(z)}\right)$, where $z=\frac\pi4(1+i)^4\left[\frac{1-\sqrt\pi i}{\sqrt\pi+i}+\frac{\sqrt\pi-i}{1+\sqrt\pi i}\right]$, $i=\sqrt{-1}$, then the distance of the point $(\alpha,\beta)$ from the line $4x-3y=7$ is ______.
questions.key_idea: Both fractions equal $\frac1i=-i$ (their numerators are $-i$ times their denominators), so $z=2\pi i$.
solution: Over the common denominator the bracket is $\frac{(1-\sqrt\pi i)(1+\sqrt\pi i)+(\sqrt\pi-i)(\sqrt\pi+i)}{(\sqrt\pi+i)(1+\sqrt\pi i)}=\frac{1+\pi+\pi+1}{i(1+\pi)-\sqrt\pi+\sqrt\pi}=\frac{2(1+\pi)}{i(1+\pi)}=\frac2i$.
So there is one solution: $\alpha=1$, and the point is $(1,4)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Spot that $1-\sqrt\pi i=-i\left(\sqrt\pi+i\right)$ and $\sqrt\pi-i=-i\left(1+\sqrt\pi i\right)$, so each fraction is exactly $-i$ with no algebra.
solution: The bracket is $-2i$, and $(1+i)^4=(2i)^2=-4$, so $z=\frac\pi4(-4)(-2i)=2\pi i$.

useful_results: Look for a numerator equal to $\pm i$ times the denominator: $\frac{1-ti}{t+i}=-i$ for any real $t$ (because $-i(t+i)=1-ti$).
$a^x=b^x$ with $a\neq b>0$ has exactly one solution, $x=0$ (take $\left(\frac ab\right)^x=1$).

concepts: Maximum and minimum of $|z-z_0|$ over a region of the Argand plane (disc cut by a half-plane)
questions.question: Let $P=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z+2-3i|\le1\}$ and $Q=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:z(1+i)+\bar z(1-i)\le-8\}$. Let in $P\cap Q$, $|z-3+2i|$ be maximum and minimum at $z_1$ and $z_2$ respectively. If $|z_1|^2+2|z_2|^2=\alpha+\beta\sqrt2$, where $\alpha,\beta$ are integers, then $\alpha+\beta$ equals ______.
questions.key_idea: $|z-3+2i|$ is the distance from $P_0(3,-2)$: the farthest point is on the line through $P_0$ and the disc's centre, the nearest is where that line (perpendicular to the boundary) meets $x-y+4=0$.
solution: $|z-3+2i|$ is the distance from the point $(3,-2)$, which lies on $L_1:x+y-1=0$ together with the centre $(-2,3)$.
The maximum $z_1$ is the intersection of the circle with $L_1$ farthest from $(3,-2)$: $L_1$ meets the circle at $z_1\left(-2-\frac1{\sqrt2},\ 3+\frac1{\sqrt2}\right)$.

The minimum $z_2$ is the intersection of $L_1$ and $L_2$ ($L_1\perp L_2$, so this is the foot of the perpendicular from $(3,-2)$ to $L_2$): solving, $z_2\left(-\frac32,\frac52\right)$, at distance $\frac1{\sqrt2}<1$ from the centre, so it lies in the disc.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use vectors: $z_1=C+\hat u$ with $\hat u$ the unit vector from $P_0$ to the centre $C$, so $|z_1|^2=|C|^2+2C\cdot\hat u+1$; and $z_2$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $P_0$ to $L_2$ by the formula, which lies inside the disc.
solution: $P_0=(3,-2)$, $C=(-2,3)$, $\hat u=\frac{C-P_0}{|C-P_0|}=\frac{(-5,5)}{5\sqrt2}=\frac{(-1,1)}{\sqrt2}$; the farthest point of the disc is $z_1=C+\hat u$.
Foot of the perpendicular from $P_0$ to $x-y+4=0$: $P_0-\frac{3+2+4}{2}(1,-1)=(3,-2)-\frac92(1,-1)=\left(-\frac32,\frac52\right)$.
This foot is at distance $\frac{1}{\sqrt2}<1$ from $C$, so it lies in the disc and is the nearest point of $P\cap Q$: $z_2=\left(-\frac32,\frac52\right)$, $|z_2|^2=\frac{17}2$.
$z_1$ is in $Q$: $y-x-4=\left(3+\frac1{\sqrt2}\right)-\left(-2-\frac1{\sqrt2}\right)-4=1+\sqrt2>0$, so the farthest point of the disc is allowed.

useful_results: Over a disc with centre $C$ and radius $r$, the distance from an outside point $P_0$ ranges over $[\,|P_0C|-r,\ |P_0C|+r\,]$, attained on line $P_0C$; for a disc cut by a half-plane, check that these points lie in the half-plane, else use the boundary line.
The nearest point of a line to $P_0$ is the foot of the perpendicular: $P_0-\frac{ax_0+by_0+c}{a^2+b^2}(a,b)$.
$z(1+i)+\bar z(1-i)=2\,\mathrm{Re}\{(1+i)z\}=2(x-y)$; $\;\alpha z+\bar\alpha\bar z$ is always real $=2\mathrm{Re}(\alpha z)$ and describes a line or half-plane.

concepts: Mean and variance with two unknown observations
questions.question: If the mean and the variance of $6,4,a,8,b,12,10,13$ are $9$ and $9.25$ respectively, then $a+b+ab$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Mean gives $a+b$, variance (via $\sum x^2$) gives $a^2+b^2$; then $ab=\frac{(a+b)^2-(a^2+b^2)}{2}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Work with deviations from the mean $9$: they sum to $0$ and their squares sum to $8\times9.25=74$; the numbers are small, and $a+b+ab=(a+1)(b+1)-1$.
solution: Deviations from $9$: $-3,-5,-1,3,1,4$ for the known values, summing to $-1$.
Sum of squares of deviations $=8\times9.25=74$; known ones give $9+25+1+9+1+16=61$, so $p^2+q^2=13$.

useful_results: Variance equals the mean of squared deviations from the mean, so shifting the origin to the mean makes the numbers small: $\sum d_i=0$ and $\sum d_i^2=n\sigma^2$.
From $s=a+b$ and $q=a^2+b^2$: $ab=\frac{s^2-q}{2}$; and $a+b+ab=(a+1)(b+1)-1$.
Check: with $a=7,b=12$ the mean is $\frac{72}{8}=9$ and $\sum x^2=722$.

concepts: Mean and variance with unknown observations; variance of $n+x_n$
questions.question: Let the mean and variance of five observations $x_1=1,x_2=3,x_3=a,x_4=7$ and $x_5=b$, $a>b$, be $5$ and $10$ respectively. Then the variance of the observations $n+x_n$, $n=1,2,\dots,5$ is:
questions.key_idea: Mean and variance fix $a+b=14$ and $a^2+b^2=116$, hence $a=10$, $b=4$; then compute the variance of $2,5,13,11,9$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use $\mathrm{Var}(x_n+n)=\mathrm{Var}(x)+\mathrm{Var}(n)+2\,\mathrm{Cov}(x,n)$ with $\mathrm{Var}(n)=2$ for $1,\dots,5$.
solution: After $a=10$, $b=4$ (from mean $5$, variance $10$): the data are $x=(1,3,10,7,4)$ against $n=(1,2,3,4,5)$.

useful_results: $\mathrm{Var}(X+Y)=\mathrm{Var}X+\mathrm{Var}Y+2\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)$ with $\mathrm{Cov}=\overline{XY}-\bar X\bar Y$; the variance of $1,\dots,n$ is $\frac{n^2-1}{12}$ ($=2$ for $n=5$).
Variance is unchanged by shifting all data by a constant and scales by $k^2$ for multiplication by $k$.
Two unknowns with given sum and sum of squares: $ab=\frac{(a+b)^2-(a^2+b^2)}2$, then solve the quadratic $t^2-(a+b)t+ab=0$.

concepts: Mean, standard deviation and mean deviation about the mode
questions.question: Let the mean and the standard deviation of the observations $2,3,3,4,5,7,a,b$ be $4$ and $\sqrt2$ respectively. Then the mean deviation about the mode of these observations is:
questions.key_idea: Mean and variance give $a+b=8$ and $a^2+b^2=32$, forcing $a=b=4$ (so the mode is $4$).
solution: The observations are $2,3,3,4,4,4,5,7$, so the mode is $4$ (it occurs three times).
Mean deviation about the mode $=\frac{2+1+1+0+1+3+0+0}{8}$ (the six listed deviations plus $|a-4|=|b-4|=0$).

alternate_solutions.idea: Variance is the mean squared deviation about the mean $4$: the six known values already contribute $16=8\sigma^2$, so $(a-4)^2+(b-4)^2=0$ at once.
solution: Deviations from the mean $4$ of the known values $2,3,3,4,5,7$: $-2,-1,-1,0,1,3$.
The mode is $4$, equal to the mean, so the mean deviation about the mode equals the mean absolute deviation about the mean $=\frac{2+1+1+0+1+3+0+0}{8}=1$: option (C).

useful_results: $n\sigma^2=\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2$: if the known data already use up $n\sigma^2$, every unknown must equal the mean.
Variance as a sum of squares: it vanishes only when every deviation is $0$; use this to solve unknowns instantly.
Mean deviation about a point $c$ is $\frac1n\sum|x_i-c|$ (absolute values); it is smallest when $c$ is the median.

concepts: Correcting the mean and standard deviation for a wrongly recorded observation
questions.question: The mean and standard deviation of $100$ observations are $40$ and $5.1$, respectively. By mistake one observation is taken as $50$ instead of $40$. If the correct mean and the correct standard deviation are $\mu$ and $\sigma$ respectively, then $10(\mu+\sigma)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Recover $\sum x_i^2$ from the old mean and variance, replace $50^2$ by $40^2$, and recompute.
questions.correction_note: PDF writes $\sigma^2=\frac{\sum x_i^2-52^2+40^2}{100}-\mu^2=25$: the square of the wrong value is $50^2$, not $52^2$ (with $52^2$ the result is $22.96$, not $25$). Its last line also reads $100(\mu+\sigma)$ where $10(\mu+\sigma)$ is meant. Corrected to $50^2$ and $10(\mu+\sigma)$; answer unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Measure deviations from $40$: the wrong value $50$ contributed $(50-40)^2=100$ to $\sum(x-40)^2$ and the correct value $40$ contributes $0$.
solution: The wrong observation $50$ contributed $(50-40)^2=100$; the correct one $40$ contributes $0$. Corrected $\sum(x_i-40)^2=2601-100=2501$.

useful_results: Variance about any reference point $c$: $\sigma^2=\frac{\sum(x_i-c)^2}{n}-(\bar x-c)^2$; choosing $c$ near the mean keeps the numbers small.
A wrong value $w$ replaced by the right value $r$ changes the mean by $\frac{r-w}{n}$ and $\sum x^2$ by $r^2-w^2$.
Recompute the mean first: the corrected mean enters the variance formula as $\mu^2$, not the old $40^2$.
